newsitem.title: UK: DEPRESSED TIN PRICE FORCES U.K. MINE TO CLOSE.
newsitem.headline: DEPRESSED TIN PRICE FORCES U.K. MINE TO CLOSE.

text.p: Depressed tin prices and a modest demand growth outlook have forced the U.K.'s last tin mine to close, which comes as little surprise, analysts said.
On Thursday, the U.K. Press Association (PA) reported that South Crofty Holdings Ltd said its tin mine in Cornwall, England, is to close down with the loss of 270 jobs.
"It is a great pity...but no great surprise," Angus MacMillan, analyst at London Metal Exchange (LME) trader Billiton Metals said.
Managers announced the closure at an emergency meeting on Thursday morning, blaming the decision on the falling price of tin on the world market and the strengthening of sterling against the dollar.
"It has had an air of inevitability about...it was one of the marginal world producers," MacMillan said.
On the LME three months tin was around $5,600 a tonne on Thursday, but last month prices were languishing at 52-month lows of $5,300.
Analyst Ted Arnold of stockbroker Merrill Lynch noted in the his latest monthly review that the rally does not appear too convincing.
Consumers buy on a hand-to-mouth basis on the view that levels above $5,600 will bring out fresh sales from major producers China and Brazil, Merrill said.
South Crofty is a small producer, with annual production of 2,100 tonnes in 1996 having been seen rising to 2,400 tonnes this year.

The company had brought its operating costs down by 12 percent from 1996 levels, but still proved vulnerable to the strength of sterling against the dollar, as South Crofty exports its production, analysts noted.
The supply/demand picture, meanwhile is not promising.
The Flemings Global Mining Group, in its latest issue of the Commodity Companion, forecast refined supply rising by 4.8 percent this year, largely due to new production from Peru kicking in.
Demand stagnated last year, and although there should be some growth in line with economic recovery, the market will be either balanced or in surplus in coming years, Flemings said.
Billiton noted that the International Tin Research Institute (ITRI) is actively exploring ways of boosting tin demand.
"...we believe this has become necessary simply to offset losses elsewhere either through substitution or miniaturisation," Billiton said.
Tin's main end-use is in electrical solders and alloys, closely followed by tinplate for beverage cans and packaging. These uses account for some 60 percent of total end-use, Flemings noted.
"Future markets include the mobile phone sector, where the demand for lead free solders could be positive," Flemings added.
